title: Heavy and Light for Grade 1: Teaching Weight Before Scales + Free Quiz
meta_title: Heavy and Light for Grade 1 (Weight) + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Teach heavy and light for Grade 1: holding, balancing and comparing weight for kids before scales, with a free 8-question quiz and printable practice.
excerpt: A six-year-old learns weight with their hands long before they meet a scale. Here is how I teach heavy and light in Grade 1, using a mango, a cotton ball and a simple balance, plus a quick quiz to test your child.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a six-year-old a mango in one palm and a cotton ball in the other, and ask which one pushes their hand down. They will not hesitate. That downward pull is the whole idea of weight, and a child feels it years before they can read a number on a scale. So when we teach heavy and light for Grade 1, the kitchen scale stays in the cupboard for a while. We start with hands.

I have watched a lot of Grade 1 children meet weight for the first time, and the ones who get it are never the ones who memorised ‘heavy means more’. They are the ones who picked things up, argued about which was heavier, and got surprised. Below is the order I actually teach it in, with things you already have at home — a mango, a cotton ball, an atta bag, a pencil box, a fistful of marbles.

Start by holding, not measuring

The first tool is the child’s own two hands. Put one object in each hand and ask a single question: which hand goes down? The hand that sinks is holding the heavier thing; the hand that rises is holding the lighter one. That is it. No numbers, no units.

Do it with pairs where the answer is obvious first — a water bottle versus a balloon, a shoe versus a sock — so the child trusts their hands. The words to keep repeating are heavier and lighter, always as a comparison between two things. A single object is not ‘heavy’ on its own in Grade 1; it is heavier than something else. That comparison habit matters more than any single answer.

The balance: a pair of hands made of wood

Once a child compares confidently by hand, the balance — the taraazu — is just a fairer, steadier pair of hands. Put one object in each pan and read the tilt. The pan that goes down holds the heavier object. The pan that goes up holds the lighter one. If the two pans sit level, the objects weigh the same.

You can build one in two minutes: a ruler balanced across a round pencil, or a coat hanger with a paper cup taped to each end. The point is not craft. The point is that the child predicts the tilt before letting go, then checks. That prediction step is where the learning happens — a child who guesses and then sees is thinking, not just watching.

Which way does it tip?

Spend real time on reading the tilt, because this is where careless mistakes live. Down means heavier. Up means lighter. Level means equal. I have seen children who understand weight perfectly still say the wrong pan is heavier simply because they read the picture too fast, so slow this down and say it out loud every time.

The big surprise: big is not always heavy

Here is the one idea that does the most work in Grade 1, and it is genuinely counter-intuitive for a six-year-old: a bigger thing is not always the heavier thing. A large balloon is bigger than a small stone, yet the stone drops your hand and the balloon barely registers. A puffy cotton ball is far bigger than a coin, and far lighter.

Children assume size and weight are the same thing because, most of the time, they are. So show them the exceptions on purpose. When a child holds a big empty box and a small full water bottle and feels the small one win, something clicks. That surprise is worth more than ten worksheets, because it forces them to trust their hands over their eyes.

The two objectsWhich looks biggerWhich is heavier
Balloon vs small stoneBalloonStone
Cotton ball vs coinCotton ballCoin
Empty box vs full water bottleBoxWater bottle
Big pillow vs atta packetPillowAtta packet

Putting things in order

After comparing two objects, the next step is lining up three. Give a child a mango, an apple and a grape and ask them to place the objects from lightest to heaviest. The trick is to compare two at a time using the balance, not to guess the whole line at once. Grape is lighter than apple; apple is lighter than mango; so the order runs grape, apple, mango.

Ordering is quietly teaching a bigger idea — that weight sits on a line, from very light to very heavy, and every object has a place on it. That is the same reasoning they will later use with a real number line, so it is worth doing patiently.

Counting the weight: non-standard units

Before grams and kilograms, children weigh things in other things. Put a pencil box in one pan of the balance and drop marbles into the other pan until the two sit level. If it takes eight marbles, then the pencil box weighs the same as eight marbles. That is a non-standard unit, and it is exactly how measurement should begin.

  • Same object, every time. Use identical marbles — if the marbles are different sizes, the count means nothing.
  • Heavier objects need more. A stapler might take twenty marbles; an eraser might take three. More marbles means heavier.
  • Compare fairly. Two objects measured in the same marbles can be ranked by their counts — fifteen marbles beats nine marbles.
  • Then swap the unit. Weigh the same pencil box in bottle caps instead. A different count for the same box shows why the world eventually agreed on kilograms.

You do not need to reach kilograms in Grade 1, and I would not rush it. A child who can balance a pencil box against a pile of marbles already understands what weighing means. The kilogram is just a marble everyone agrees on, and that comes later.

A gentle word on kilograms

You will see ‘kg’ printed on the atta bag and the child will ask. That is fine — tell them it is a heavier weight that shops use, and that a bag of atta is a couple of kilograms while a marble is far, far less. But do not build lessons around the number yet. In Grade 1, the goal is the feeling and the comparison. Grams and kilograms are Grade 2 and 3 work, and they land much better once the hands already know what heavy means.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a short, free quiz on exactly what we covered — heavier and lighter, which way the balance tips, the big-is-not-always-heavy surprise, and ordering by weight. Every question is worded so your child can answer it by picturing the objects, no image needed. Let them try, then read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for written practice, the printable worksheet at the end has graded weight questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 1 Heavy and Light Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on comparing weight, reading a balance and ordering objects. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 1 heavy and light — comparing weight

questions.q: You hold a mango in one hand and a cotton ball in the other. Which hand goes down?
questions.explanation: The heavier object pulls the hand down. A mango is much heavier than a cotton ball, so the mango hand sinks.

questions.q: On a balance, one pan goes down and the other goes up. Which object is heavier?
options: The one in the pan that went up
The one in the pan that went down
questions.explanation: The pan that goes down holds the heavier object. Down means heavier, up means lighter.

questions.q: A big balloon and a small stone are placed on a balance. Which side goes down?
options: The bigger side always goes down
questions.explanation: Big is not always heavy. The small stone is heavier than the large balloon, so the stone side goes down.

questions.q: Both pans of a balance sit perfectly level. What does that tell you?
options: The two objects weigh the same
questions.explanation: When the pans are level, neither object pulls harder, so they weigh the same.

questions.q: A pencil box balances exactly against 8 marbles. A book balances against 15 of the same marbles. Which is heavier?
options: You need a real scale to know
questions.explanation: More marbles means heavier. 15 marbles is more than 8, so the book is heavier than the pencil box.

questions.q: Put these in order from lightest to heaviest: a grape, a mango, an apple.
questions.explanation: A grape is lightest, a mango is heaviest, and the apple sits in between: grape, apple, mango.
A feather barely pushes your hand down at all, so it is the lightest of the four.

questions.q: An empty box looks bigger than a small full water bottle. Which is heavier?
options: The empty box, because it is bigger
questions.explanation: Size is not weight. The empty box is light even though it is big, and the full water bottle is heavier.

faq.q: How do I explain heavy and light to a Grade 1 child?
faq.a: Give them one object in each hand and ask which hand goes down. The hand that sinks holds the heavier thing. Comparing by feel, with words like heavier and lighter, teaches weight far better than any definition at this age.

faq.q: Should I use a real weighing scale in Grade 1?
faq.a: Not yet. A simple balance — a taraazu, or even a ruler on a pencil — teaches which object is heavier without any numbers. Grams and kilograms come in Grade 2 and 3, once the child already understands what weighing means.

faq.q: My child thinks the bigger object is always heavier. How do I fix that?
faq.a: Show them the exceptions on purpose. Let them hold a big balloon and a small stone, or a puffy cotton ball and a coin. Feeling the smaller object win the tug is the surprise that breaks the size-equals-weight idea.

faq.q: What are non-standard units for weight?
faq.a: They are everyday objects used to measure, like marbles or bottle caps. If a pencil box balances against 8 identical marbles, it weighs the same as 8 marbles. This is how measurement should begin — counting weight in things before using grams.
